blocks.text: 1. The big picture

In Spanish the ending of the verb tells you who is doing the action. Every verb in its dictionary form (the infinitive) ends in -ar, -er or -ir. Take that ending off to get the stem, then add the ending that matches the person.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: hablar (to speak): stem habl- + ending -o = hablo (I speak)
Regular verbs follow one fixed pattern per group, so learning three sets of endings lets you conjugate hundreds of verbs.

blocks.title: Spain vs Latin America
blocks.text: In Spain you say vosotros to a group of friends or family and ustedes only to a group you address formally. In Latin America ustedes is used for both, so you will hear it a lot in videos and apps. This course always includes vosotros.

blocks.title: Leave the pronoun out
blocks.text: The ending already shows the person, so Spanish normally drops the subject pronoun: Hablo español, not Yo hablo español. Use a pronoun only for contrast or emphasis: Yo hablo inglés, pero ella habla francés. (I speak English, but she speaks French.) Él, ella and usted share one verb form, so a pronoun or a name can also remove doubt.
3. The endings
Learn these three columns. The stem never changes for regular verbs.

blocks.title: Patterns worth memorising
bullets: The yo form always ends in -o, in all three groups.
-er and -ir verbs have the same endings except for nosotros (-emos / -imos) and vosotros (-éis / -ís).
The only written accents in regular present-tense forms are in the vosotros forms: habláis, coméis, vivís.
The stress falls on the stem in yo, tú, él and ellos forms (HAblo, HAblas, HAbla, HAblan) and on the ending in nosotros and vosotros forms (hablAmos, habLÁIS).

All of these follow the patterns above exactly. Practise them aloud with all six persons.

blocks.title: Not in these lists on purpose
blocks.text: Verbs like ser, estar, ir, tener, hacer, ver and stem-changers like poder, querer, dormir are irregular in the present tense. They are in the next PDF.
6. When do you use the present tense?

head: Use
Example
English
rows: I work from Monday to Friday.
Do you speak English? Yes, I speak a little.

blocks.title: Good news for Dutch speakers
blocks.text: Spanish, like Dutch, often uses the present tense for the near future (Mañana trabajo = Morgen werk ik). Also, one Spanish form covers both English forms: hablo means I speak and I am speaking.

Siempre bebo agua. — I always drink water.
A veces escucho música. — Sometimes I listen to music.
Nunca como carne. — I never eat meat.

blocks.title: Negatives and questions in one line
blocks.text: Put no before the verb for a negative: No hablo francés. For a question, put the sentence between ¿ and ? and raise your voice at the end: ¿Hablas inglés? Full details come in A1 · PDF 8.
7. Common mistakes

rows: Conjugate the verb. The infinitive is not used after a subject.
Yo trabajo, yo estudio y yo vivo en Madrid.
Trabajo, estudio y vivo en Madrid.
Dutch needs ik/jij every time. Spanish endings already show the person.
Vosotros: -er verbs take -éis. The ending -ís belongs only to -ir verbs (vivís).
Ustedes (formal plural) uses the ellos/ellas form.
Tú always ends in -s. Él/ella/usted has no -s.
Usted is formal and takes the él/ella form, not the tú form.
